pitch_detail.notes: Climb to the right of the big roof near the start. Going left at the roof is an easier variation at about 5.9. Gear tops out around 3 inches.
A mostly finger-width crack leads up the wall. Near the top you traverse rightward past a single bolt.

review.changed: Wrote both pitches. Per-pitch grades are not stated, so the route grade is used on both; the 5.9 left-hand variation at the roof is noted. No lengths or anchors given. No rappel table. (Reviewer: per-pitch grades removed; the text states none.)

pitch_detail.notes: A low-angle left-facing corner takes you to a stance beneath a large square roof.
Go up and over the roof on its right side, then follow shallow flaring cracks, including a short offwidth section, to a stance at the foot of the big left-facing corner.
The huge left-facing dihedral is heavily vegetated. Near its top, move out left to a belay close to a short chimney where the fourth-class ground begins.
Fourth-class travel up a grassy gully and corner to a wide grassy ledge below the steep tower. The finish variations (Thin Mint and Godiva, both 5.8) start from this ledge.
Traverse leftward along the grassy ledge, then work upward through the obvious weak lines on the tower's western side, stopping where the steep final headwall starts.
Left-slanting cracks lead up the headwall to the top. About a hundred feet of third-class scrambling then reaches the true summit.

review.changed: Wrote all six pitches. No lengths or bolts stated; the text says there is no fixed gear or bolt anchors, so no anchor field set. No rappel table (walk-off descent).
review.other_findings: Text says an easy walk-off to east or west.

pitch_detail.notes: Start from the boulder-flake cave on a steep left-trending ramp, then work right toward the shallow corner-crack below the roofs. Follow the corner to the first roof and pull it on the right. A first anchor sits just past that roof, a cramped spot under the second roof. Continue up and right to a roomier two-bolt anchor beside the second roof. A perched flake above that belay may be loose.

review.changed: Wrote pitch 1 only; pitch 2 is not described beyond a sling anchor at its top. No rappel table: the text discusses options for rappelling but not station by station.
review.other_findings: Pitch 1 is described as about 5.9 whereas the route grade is 5.10a, so the harder grade presumably lies on pitch 2.

pitch_detail.notes: Slab with gear in the overlaps and in a left-facing corner. When that corner is damp, step left and wander up the slab alongside it. Serious on the gear.
More gear-protected slab. A big runout on good holds passes one bolt, then the line trends left beneath a large roof, where gear goes in the overlap.

Place a big cam, then commit to a rock-over past the roof's left end and step right onto a slab with sparse handholds but decent footholds. After clipping a bolt, a steep wall of excellent incut holds runs out to an overlap that accepts small gear. Positive face climbing with spaced but reasonable protection finishes the pitch.
Head straight for the top of the cliff on good incut holds with generally solid gear.

review.changed: Wrote all four pitches. Pitches 1-3 are marked R in the text; this is mentioned in notes only for P1-P3 wording. No rappel table: text only says the four belays have rap rings.
review.other_findings: Pitch lengths sum to 215 m, close to the stored 213 m.

pitch_detail.notes: Two ways in: traverse right on big easy holds to the main corner and climb to a roof about 80 feet up, then go left toward a slung flake that works as an intermediate belay, or go straight up cracks on the right of the ledge to that flake. From just above the flake, drift back to the corner and continue to the belay.

Take the left side of the pillar in the main corner (the right side is a wide 5.9 option). It looks improbable from below, but stemming, laybacking and face moves with good holds and plentiful gear make it work.

Often wet. Climb the watery corner past a pin about 40 feet up, which is a retreat point. After 60-70 feet you meet a series of roofs; just under the second, cross left on face holds to another corner and follow it to the belay. The topo grade is 5.10b, but it felt closer to 5.9 even wet.
Keep following the corner with good climbing and good protection to a roomy ledge, the first comfortable belay stance on the route.
Scramble right on easy ground, then back left into the corner. The first 60 feet are about 5.0 and out of the belayer's sight. Higher, gear thins out and the climbing gets harder.

Climb the corner for about 100 feet, then traverse right toward the arete. Cracks and seams just before the arete take plenty of gear and are the better choice than going around the arete. Long ropes are needed, with a little simul-climbing possible.

Traverse up and right to stem on large vertical flakes, then continue up and right through several crack and small-corner options. The line is hard to pin down; expect ledges on the right in the final third.

Awkward from the start, with broken cracks across slabs. Find gear in a flake on the left, then trend up and right over a slab on a pillar that faces left. Build an anchor at the base of the hanging flake with small to medium cams.

The crux. Layback the left side of the hanging flake as the crack narrows from fingers to a seam, then traverse left under the roof where good handholds appear. Go up the next corner about 10 feet to an anchor of a few nuts and a large cam. Strong parties could link this with pitch 8 on a 70 m rope.

An outstanding stemming corner, sustained for 120-150 feet, then easier for another 30 feet to a gravelly ledge. Beware loose rocks over the belayer. A rappel anchor of slings between two leaning rocks sits about 20 feet higher and can serve as the belay.

Moderate but wandering mountain terrain, around 200 feet including walking. Go up a rounded corner on crumbly feet to a flat gravelly ledge, then up a corner system with a crack along its left edge, to a belay on a dirty low-angle ledge between a flake and the wall.

Easy ground, roughly 150 feet of which about 100 is horizontal walking. Head up and slightly right toward a wide corner made by two large boulders, stem through to a small roof, then traverse right to top out. A few feet of blocky scrambling, unroped, reaches the summit.

review.changed: Wrote all 12 pitches; feet converted to metres. Pitches 11 and 12 have no grade stated (described as easy mountain terrain), so grade omitted. Approach snow/ledge pitch (p0) and the start ledge are left out of the table. Belays are described as mostly fixed wires, pins and slings with one bolted station; not set per pitch since the text does not say which. No rappel table.
review.other_findings: Text says P3 felt about 5.9 versus the 5.10b topo grade.

pitch_detail.notes: Climb the slabby dihedral, then wander rightward to a stance on a ledge with a bolted belay. One bolt and one piton protect it.

Leave the belay heading left up steeper rock to the bolted crux. Past it, exit an alcove rightward onto a grassy ledge beneath a big left-facing corner. Five bolts and a piton protect the pitch. The belay there is built from gear, and a number 3 cam helps.

review.changed: Wrote both pitches; feet converted to metres. Further pitches above the end of the route are mentioned but not described, so left out. No rappel table.
review.other_findings: Stored length 61 m is shorter than the 70 ft + 125 ft (about 59 m) total, consistent.

pitch_detail.notes: Scramble left along the ramp to the foot of the crack. Steep, friendly 5.8 climbing leads to a stiff roof move protected by steel nuts. The roof can be skirted on the right, which holds the route to 5.10a.
Easy climbing up to an exit move out of the corner.
Walk the clean ramp to a broad, shallow-angle dihedral that has a single bolt. Thin cracks above lead to an airy finish at 5.9.

review.changed: Wrote all three pitches. No lengths or per-pitch anchors given (bolted anchors in general). No rappel table: only 'rappel with a single 60 m rope or scramble off'.

pitch_detail.notes: Belay from the ledge at the top of the gully. Start on a diagonal crack running right to left up the face and follow the obvious flake to a belay in blocks at its top left.

Climb left over blocks away from the belay and cross easy terrain. Get on the ridge proper as soon as it allows; trending left is easier but the buttress line hugs the ridge, and the climbing there is fun and moderate.
Stay close to the ridgeline.
More 5.6 terrain along the ridge.
Go slightly down and left of the main corner and roof above the belay ledge, then up the left side of the ridge to a big ledge.
Up the face slightly left of the ridge to an exposed traverse across a short flake. Downclimb its left side, then climb a corner with good feet and a few tricky moves. Belay above the roof or block.
Easy ground onto several huge ledges in a row. The first or second makes a roomy bivy spot. Belay from the lowest ledge.

The best pitch. From the lowest of three ledges, climb an easy blocky pitch to the next ledge, then follow a shallow offwidth-like crack on the right of the face above the second ledge. Traverse past the end of the ledge to the right side of the ridge with big exposure, then easy climbing into blocks. Rope drag can be severe, so plan protection carefully. Trending left of the ridge is a slightly easier, less exposed option.
Easy ground with plentiful gear onto a large slab. Belay from a slung block around the back of its upper right corner. Hard cracks, perhaps 5.10-5.11, line the big face to the right.
Turn right around the back of the ridge and follow a loose blocky ramp to the summit slabs.

review.changed: Wrote all 10 pitches. No lengths, bolts or anchors given (route has no bolts). Rappel: only 'rap pitches 10, 9, 8 then trend into the bowl' with slung chockstones, not a station list; no rappel table.
review.other_findings: Pitch 9 grade is given as 5.0 or 4th class.

pitch_detail.notes: Cross the bergschrund where possible and climb fifth-class ground to reach fourth-class terrain below a prominent left-facing corner on the buttress.
Fourth-class terrain to the base of the left-facing corner below the headwall.
Climb the left-facing corner, with 5.10a moves near its top, to reach a left-trending ramp and traverse leading to a pillar at the foot of the main headwall. Belay in a notch in the pillar.
A short traverse to the bottom of the pillar beneath the headwall.
A short handcrack in a flare gains the top of the pillar.
First headwall pitch: obvious finger cracks from the top of the pillar to the next ledge.
A clear hand crack splits a small roof; above it, cracks slant slightly left to a big ledge at the headwall's left edge. Graded 5.8/9.
A short left-facing corner gains the top of the headwall and the ridge leading to the summit.

review.changed: Wrote the 8 pitches the text lists; about 500 ft of 4th/5th-class ridge above is not a numbered pitch and is left out. The text notes the first three pitches include simul-climbing and likely split into more. No lengths, bolts or anchors. No rappel table: descent beta is a narrative.
review.other_findings: Stored 10 pitches vs 8 listed; the author says the lower pitches likely break into more.

pitch_detail.notes: A shallow-angle dihedral facing left leads to a belay in a notch among boulders, where fixed rappel slings hang.

Scramble up and right through a notch, then climb the slightly overhanging splitter crack, sized for a number 1 cam. It bends right and narrows to fingers with big exposure. Belay from slings at the top of the flake, or go 10 more feet up an easy fifth-class crack to the summit and downclimb. It could be aided at C1.

review.changed: Wrote both pitches; feet converted to metres; P1 grade given as 5.6-5.7, recorded as 5.7. No rappel table: single 60 m rappel from fixed slings only.
review.other_findings: Text says the crux is no harder than about 5.11b, while the first ascent party gave 5.12a/b.

pitch_detail.notes: Flakes lead to a little roof in a corner; move left onto a second crack and continue up a brief chimney to a belay on a pillar top. Jamming directly through the roof on perfect hands is a 5.10 alternative.

A classic. From over the belay, a finger and hand crack heads leftward to an alcove, and an outstanding jam crack then takes a steep face to a ledge with a chain anchor. This can be linked with the first pitch.
Corners and easy ground trending rightward to the next anchor.
Move right of the anchor behind a flake and take a good corner to a roof. Traverse beneath it rightward into another corner and pull over a second roof to a chained belay ledge on your left.
Cracks on the face to the right lead into a corner and up to another ledge.
A steep corner, then scramble left around the arete and go up a face to the ridge crest for the belay.

review.changed: Wrote all six pitches. No lengths or bolt counts. No rappel table: the descent is a shared rappel line on another route, not stations of this one.

pitch_detail.notes: Begin roughly 10 feet to the left of a big left-facing dihedral, following finger cracks. Two overhangs block the way: avoid the first by going around its left, the second around its right. Belay on a small stance just past the second.
Cracks and face climbing lead to a steeper upper wall, where you belay.
Keep climbing the face, angling rightward to a chimney that is a struggle, and belay at its top. A hand crack to the right reaches the same stance if you prefer to skip the chimney.
Step right and climb a steep cracked corner, getting perfect hands through a roof. Once over the roof, belay in a crack on the left.
Awkward finger to fist cracks straight up to the top of the ridge.

review.changed: Wrote all five pitches. The text says every pitch is rated 5.10 (per a guidebook), so 5.10 is used on each, with the crux on pitch 4. No lengths. Only one bolted belay exists (top of the chimney). No rappel table: rappels follow another route's line.

pitch_detail.notes: Climb easy, blocky terrain up the southeast flank of the Matriarch. The pitch ends with a very exposed move up and left from a small notch.
Scramble along the ridge to a short, perfect hand crack that is closer to 5.8.

Stroll along the ridge, rappelling briefly where needed, and surmount a blank section on a short bolt ladder. Drop down the far side to a big chockstone. At its base, the leader either climbs the single move back up, or does it while being lowered, which needs care. Watch for rope snags beneath the chockstone.
A bolt-protected au cheval is straddled, then slabs lie beyond. A short rappel down a groove follows, often snowy into late season.

Descend by scrambling and cross over to Grimface, then bear right to chimneys that go upward. Merge with the southeast notch route and follow the easiest line, chimneys and blocky ground, to the summit.

review.changed: Wrote the five entries the text gives (pitches 5 and 6 are combined). The text calls the description approximate. No rappel table: '3 or 4 rappels' only, with a couple of short ones mentioned in pitches.

pitch_detail.notes: Clip the starting bolt and do a few moves, then follow the slim, shallow right-facing corner on the pillar's right side. Sustained thin hands at 5.9 lead to a bolted belay atop the pillar. Early in the season the first half may be under snow.

Head right on quartz holds, clip a bolt, then a few thin crux moves get you over a flake. More face moves then aim for big left-facing flakes, wet early in the season. Belay at bolts atop a large jutting flake.
Excellent. Go left up a steep finger-hand crack, pull the bulge, and follow the long splitter up the slab. At its end move right past two bolts to a bolted belay. The original start joins here.
Follow the broad ramp to its end, with easy climbing on poor rock and the best protection in cracks on the left. At the top of the ramp, cross an unprotected slab to the right to a slung horn belay.
A steep, fingery stemming corner, dirty and loose at the top but fun lower. The upper half of the Sprung C*ck Erect variation breaks right here.

A mostly horizontal leftward traverse through an odd offwidth with blind protection at the back, past chossy edges and some loose flakes. The reported slung block belay was absent, so the climber continued roughly 10 feet up to the foot of the splitter cracks.

pitch_detail.anchor: alcove next to a dead tree
pitch_detail.notes: The burly pitch. Follow splitter cracks to an offwidth pod and the orange roof under the headwall. Cupped hands or fists get you over the roof, then steep, pumpy climbing continues past a large ledge to an alcove belay by a dead tree. Both number 3 and 4 cams were used.
Juggy flakes traverse due left under an overhang to a flat ledge with a couple of trees.
A fun fingercrack in a corner to a short, reachy crux, then mostly 5.10- on juggy flakes, moving right to a two-bolt belay on a slab.
Traverse right, then work up the slab by way of cracks and shallow corners to a flat perch out on the right, with big exposure below.

Stout late in the day. A couple of steep moves, then a low-angle blocky corner with the face dropping away on the right. It steepens and takes thin gear before easing to third class. A belay bolt on the slab is unnecessary; better spots lie just beyond.
Unrope or simul the narrow blocky ridge, about 60 m of third and fourth class. It narrows to fifth class: scoot or hand-traverse the very exposed knife edge to the first rappel station on the left.

rappel_detail.station: Top of the descent gully: slung block with a nut and piton
rappel_detail.notes: Rope-stretching rappel down to an anchor of three fixed nuts.
Lands on a large ledge; downclimb leftward to a small tree. Tricky under early-season snow, but other trees allow shorter intermediate raps.
Lands on a large terrace; scramble down and a bit left to a small tree hidden behind a big white block.

rappel_detail.station: Small tree behind the white block
rappel_detail.notes: Goes down the waterfall slabs, moving hard to the right across the stream to a big slung block.
Late season this is a full 60 m to talus, with an optional 10 m rap off a pinch point on the left. Early season, a 30 m rap reaches moderate snow, with a bollard used for the steepest frozen part.

review.changed: Wrote all 12 pitch entries (pitches 4 and 5 combined as the text does). Original orange-ramp start is skipped; the described start is the harder variation. Rappel table written from the two-60 m rope sequence given in the descent beta; the single-70 m approach improvised extra stations and is not tabulated.
review.other_findings: Text says the first-three-pitch variation, not the original start, is described.

pitch_detail.notes: The big left-facing corner leads to a comfortable ledge with a sling belay.
Continue upward beyond a rappel station to a small ledge under a steeper face.
Angle left on detached flakes, then hand-traverse right to a small ledge. A short face and an easier left-facing corner lead to a fixed anchor belay.
Follow cracks up to the left end of a triangular roof, then angle right and back left to a bolted belay under the big roof. The rock is poor and protection thin (PG13).
Traverse left beneath the roof on underclings and small footholds, then climb left-facing laybacks, watching for rope drag. Belay just short of the gray ledge that slopes downward.
Angle up left and face-climb dark rock to a large ledge, about 15-20 m.
Climb to the left-facing flakes; easier going through steep flakes leads to a belay in a small alcove.
Straight up to a small ledge, then angle left to a left-facing corner. Easier climbing ends with a last mantle onto fifth-class terrain.
Fifth-class ground to the summit of Gimli.

review.changed: Wrote all nine pitches. Pitch 6 length stated as a range so no lengthM. No rappel table (descent is the East Ridge downclimb).

pitch_detail.notes: Start left of the pack-stash ledge on delicate but easy slabs, roughly 20 feet from the main crack system's left side. Take the excellent white corner, getting past a roof with strenuous pulls out to the right. About 35 m up, a flake carries a cluster of slings and rings that serve as a rappel anchor; a ledge slightly higher is the better belay, with gear in the main crack on its left. Beware of the hollow horizontal crack on that ledge. Harder than a typical 5.8 by the climber's account.
Thin cracks and dark banded-gneiss holds reach the ridge, about 5.7 to begin and easing off. Belay at a notch with a gendarme and a slung chockstone.
More steep, tricky banded gneiss to a tree and a good ledge on the ridge.
Steep and beautiful, with one hard lieback move, ending on the grassy, comfortable Lunch Ledge.
Fun and exposed climbing to the foot of the notorious roof pitch.
A short corner leads up to the roof move; go left around the roof to a small ledge. The roof move is about 5.10a.
The last fifth-class pitch: about 200 feet of nicely sculpted rock to a belay below the diving board.

review.changed: Wrote all seven pitches. Pitch 1 grade not stated, so omitted (only compared to 5.8 and 5.9 benchmarks). No rappel table.

pitch_detail.notes: Start from a ledge 10 m right of the gully between the two summits, above a short green wall, and climb the prow of a broad grey buttress.
Go up and left past a small pine and the left side of a 5 m detached pillar, then on to a lovely hand crack in a shallow corner facing right, ending near a small overhang.
A thin crack with two fixed pitons, then the steep wall along the thin crack past five bolts. Beautifully exposed.
A corner facing right, with a small bolt-protected roof near its top. Tougher than it appears.
Trad pitch up and left on easier ground to the summit. Watch for large loose blocks.

review.changed: Wrote all five pitches; every belay is bolted per the text. Pitch 5 grade not stated. No rappel table: only 'every station is bolted, rappel with two ropes'.

skip_reasons.ak_gapers_on_the_pipe_at_dawn: Text describes only pitches 2 and 3 loosely, no pitch 1, no grades or lengths; not one-by-one.
skip_reasons.ak_mt_huntington_the_harvard_route: Narrative of a 30-pitch route with grouped sections (five rope lengths, three pitches, etc.), not a pitch-by-pitch table; rappels only counted, not station by station.
